newsitem.title: ITALY: RALLYING-SAN REMO RALLY COULD DECIDE MANUFACTURERS' TITLE.
newsitem.headline: RALLYING-SAN REMO RALLY COULD DECIDE MANUFACTURERS' TITLE.

text.p: Although Finn Tommi Makinen has won the 1996 world rally drivers' title with two events to spare, Italy's San Remo rally will be one of the most hotly fought of the year.
Makinen's team Mitsubishi will try to steal the prestigious manufacturers' title from under the noses of their bigger rivals, Subaru.

Subaru have fielded the biggest team all season, running three cars in most events, but Mitsubishi take a slender nine-point advantage to Italy despite having concentrated their efforts entirely on Makinen so far.
Scenting a prestigious double success, Mitsubishi have signed Frenchman Didier Auriol -- a Subaru driver earlier in the year -- to turn up the heat on their rivals.

Auriol has three San Remo wins to his credit, which is more than all his rivals put together, but he has had little testing in the Mitsubishi car and could struggle to make the most of his feel for the terrain.
Covering 1,950 kilometres, the San Remo event is the last major rally to include high-speed stages on both asphalt and dirt roads.

It also has some of the longest stages in the world championship, with two attempts at a daunting 47-km test on the first day of competition, Monday. Unpredictable weather and varied conditions make it one of the most open rallies.
Subaru driver and 1995 world champion Colin McRae reckons that the Monday stages in central Italy will be crucial.
"They're long and I think everybody will push quite hard to try and get a bit of a lead," the Scot said.

Subaru have developed new tyres for these stages with Pirelli but McRae thinks that the asphalt mountain stages close to San Remo could be just as important, particularly if bad weather lingers and rain sweeps mud, rocks and leaves on to the roads.
"If it's wet, it won't be nice. They're not difficult stages but they're nasty and it's so easy just to hit a rock and get a puncture," he warned.
McRae predicts that Makinen will race ahead on the dirt stages on the first two days but could lose his advantage on the asphalt.

"Obviously the manufacturers' title is the most important thing now, so we'll be keeping a good eye on that," McRae said. "It's a rally we can win and I think I find it easier to adapt to different conditions than some of the others."
Ford should be a threat on roads that give good grip and suit their Escort. They also have two San Remo experts in Spaniard Carlos Sainz and Belgium's Bruno Thiry.
